newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Tajik govt says rebel colonel agreed to step down.
newsitem.headline: Tajik govt says rebel colonel agreed to step down.

text.p: The Tajik government said on Wednesday a rebel army colonel had agreed to be relieved of his command and withdraw his forces to barracks after four days of fighting around the capital Dushanbe.

The statement from President Imomali Rakhmonov's office followed peace talks between Rakhmonov and maverick Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev, who had moved troops of his elite brigade towards Dushanbe on Saturday after clashes broke out between two rival warlords.

There was no comment from the rebel colonel himself, whose troops abandoned their positions on Wednesday in the Fakhrobad valley where they had come under repeated rocket attack from forces loyal to Rakhmonov.
Shell casings and spent rockets coated the road through the scorched fields in the valley, 25 km (15 miles) south of Dushanbe, where tired government troops said all was quiet.
"Khudoyberdyev has resigned as commander of his brigade and will work in another post," Rakhmonov's spokesman Zafar Saidov told Reuters.
"All questions between both sides have been resolved on peaceful lines. Makhmud Khudoyberdyev agreed without any conditions to move all his forces back to barracks."

Saidov said Khudoyberdyev had made the concessions during two telephone conversations with Rakhmonov and that his troops had already returned to their base in Kurgan Tyube, about 110 km (70 miles) south of Dushanbe.

He said the two men did not meet personally, but official sources said they had met at the headquarters of the Russian peacekeepers in the capital of the former Soviet republic, which borders Afghanistan.
Rakhmonov later issued a decree replacing Khudoyberdyev with 30-year-old Lieutenant Colonel Sherali Mirzoyev "in connection with a transfer to other work", a presidential official said.
But he did not specify what post, if any, Khudoyberdyev had received and the colonel's headquarters in Kurgan Tyube, contacted by telephone, declined comment.
"Khudoyberdyev has flexed his muscles and won concessions before but my feeling is that this time he miscalculated," a Western diplomat said on condition of anonymity.
Russia is worried about unrest along its unstable southern rim and deploys 20,000 troops as the bulk of a Commonwealth of Independent States peace force in Tajikistan.

Moscow reacted cautiously to the new fighting, which broke out close on the heels of a four-year-long civil war involving Tajikistan's Islamic opposition. Officials insisted the peacekeepers would avoid any role in the latest conflict, but they appeared to have mediated behind the scenes.
For Khudoyberdyev, the 34-year-old politically ambitious commander of an elite government armoured brigade, the future looked unclear.
He had mutinied twice before in as many years and been a vociferous critic of a peace deal Rakhmonov signed in June with the armed Islamic opposition to end the civil war.
He moved his armour towards Dushanbe at the weekend, sparking fighting with presidential forces, after fighting erupted between two warlords in the capital.
Khudoyberdyev said on Tuesday he had no plans to take Dushanbe and that he had been provoked by what he called the presidential guard's move on his territory in the south.
He lost control of a strategically important aluminium smelter west of Dusnabe to the presidential guard on Monday.

The new fighting was not linked to the Islamist opposition but it cast further doubt on Rakhmonov's already weak grip on power, leaving the impverished central Asian republic bordering China and Afghanistan far from the stability craved by its 5.7 million population.
Gun law has carved up Tajikistan into a patchwork of independent fiefdoms under the control of armed groups like those in neighbouring Afghanistan.
